title: Building the Implementation Project Plan: From Scope to Scheduled Delivery
excerpt: A practitioner's guide to building a real HCM implementation plan: work breakdown, milestones, critical path, payroll-cycle constraints, and schedule control.

content.text: Every HCM implementation eventually faces the same uncomfortable meeting: someone asks whether the go-live date is real, and the room goes quiet. The date was set in a sales cycle or a steering deck months ago, the work was never broken down against it, and the project is discovering — week by week — that the date was a wish with a calendar attached.

Building a real plan is the moment scope gets translated into time, people, and sequencing — and where the trade-offs the sponsor will eventually face become visible early enough to act on. Here is how professional teams build it: work breakdown, milestones and gates, dependencies and the critical path, estimation, resource loading, immovable constraints, and keeping the plan honest once work starts.
What a Project Plan Actually Is — and What It Isn't

A project plan is not a list of dates. It is the documented logic connecting approved scope to scheduled delivery: what work exists, what order it must happen in, who does it, how long it takes, and which decisions confirm progress. Dates are the output of that logic, not the input. Starting from a fixed go-live date and working backward without testing whether the work fits produces a promise, not a plan.

That distinction is what lets a plan survive challenge: sponsors ask for earlier dates, scope expands, resources leave. A plan built forward from the work answers with evidence — the dependency chain behind the end date, what compressing it costs, what scope must defer.
Start with the Work Breakdown Structure

Every defensible plan starts with a work breakdown structure (WBS): the total scope decomposed into manageable pieces. For HCM implementations, the natural first cut is phase by workstream — each phase of the delivery methodology crossed with the continuous workstreams (project management, solution design and configuration, data migration, integrations, testing, change management and training, cutover). A good work package is estimable in days or weeks, owned by one person, with a clear done criterion.

The WBS enforces the 100% rule: the children of any element must account for all of that element's work — nothing in scope left out, nothing duplicated. This is where amateur plans fail quietly: data cleansing estimated at zero because "the client handles data," hypercare staffing forgotten until go-live week. Walking the breakdown with every workstream lead and asking "what's missing" is the cheapest quality control the project will ever buy.
Milestones and Phase Gates

Milestones are the plan's decision points: zero-duration markers that say something important is true. Design baseline signed. Build complete. UAT accepted. Go-live. They consume no time and no resources — they mark the moments the project formally agrees it is ready for the next thing. A plan with tasks but no milestones is a schedule with no way to declare progress.

Each milestone between phases is guarded by a gate — the entry and exit criteria from the methodology. The gate gives the milestone teeth: "UAT accepted" means signed acceptance and zero unresolved critical defects, not a feeling that testing went well. And space milestones at every phase boundary, so the hard conversations happen while there is still time to act — which is the entire point of planning.

content.alt: Layered diagram showing how an implementation plan is built: the work breakdown structure by phase feeds zero-duration milestones, each guarded by entry and exit gate criteria
content.caption: How an implementation plan is built: the WBS feeds zero-duration milestones, each guarded by entry and exit gate criteria.

content.text: Dependencies and the Critical Path

With work broken down and milestones set, the plan needs sequencing logic: dependencies. Most HCM dependencies are finish-to-start (configuration must finish before system testing begins), but the others matter too. Start-to-start links configuration cycles with data trial loads that can overlap once begun; finish-to-finish ties training completion to the UAT exit it must not outrun. Linking everything finish-to-start produces a serial plan for work that could overlap — stretching the timeline and hiding real options.

Once dependencies are set, the schedule reveals its critical path: the longest chain of dependent work, which determines the earliest the project can finish. Everything off the path has float — slack that absorbs delay without moving the end date. This is the single most useful thing a schedule produces: crashing a non-critical task buys nothing, while a two-week delay on the critical path moves go-live by two weeks, full stop. Recompute it every status cycle — the path shifts as work progresses.

content.alt: Timeline diagram of four parallel HCM workstreams — design, data migration, integrations, testing — converging on milestones, with the critical path highlighted in blue
content.caption: Four parallel HCM workstreams converging on milestones, with the critical path highlighted in blue.

content.text: Estimating Durations and Loading Resources

Durations come from the people doing the work, never from the calendar. For each work package the owner estimates effort, and the plan converts effort to duration through availability — ten person-days from someone half-allocated takes four weeks, not two. Three-point estimation (optimistic, most likely, pessimistic) forces the conversation past single-number guesses and flags which estimates carry the most uncertainty; those get revisited first when the schedule slips.

Resource loading is where plans meet reality. Build a resource calendar — availability, holidays, known blackouts — and load named people against it, not roles. Two tasks assigned to the same person in the same week is a conflict the plan should surface before week one. And sequence around contention explicitly: where one person is the bottleneck across workstreams, the schedule is fiction unless their work is sequenced.
Scheduling Around Immovable Constraints

Some dates do not negotiate. Payroll cycles are the classic immovable constraint: in a cross-border US/Canada deployment, for example, parallel payroll testing must align with both countries' processing calendars, and a missed parallel run cannot simply happen "next week" — the next window is a full cycle away. Year-end is a hard blackout for most payroll go-lives; fiscal boundaries, benefits enrollment, and union contract dates can each pin a go-live window shut.

Treat these as schedule anchors, not footnotes. Work backward from the payroll calendar to place testing windows, then fit the remaining work around them — and build the constraint list with the client's payroll and HR operations leads, not just the project team. They know the calendar the project must live inside.
Baselining, Then Controlling the Schedule

Once the plan is built, reviewed, and approved, it becomes the baseline: the agreed reference every status report measures against. Baselining is a governance act — steering approves it the way it approves scope — done once, deliberately, before execution begins in earnest.

Schedule control is the weekly discipline of comparing actual progress to the baseline: percent complete, milestones met or missed, critical-path variance, updated forecasts. A two-week slip found in week three is a resourcing conversation; found in week ten, it is a crisis. Re-baselining should be rare, explicit, and approved, and it must never be silent: moving dates without a recorded decision is how projects "stay green" all the way to a failed go-live.

content.label: Build the plan in six moves
content.intro: A defensible schedule is built in a fixed order. Click through the six moves, in sequence — each one feeds the next.

items.title: 1 · Break down the work
items.text: Build the WBS with the workstream leads: phase by workstream, every package estimable, one owner each, clear done criteria. Run the what's-missing review before any dates are set.

items.title: 2 · Set the milestones and gates
items.text: Place zero-duration milestones at every phase boundary and attach entry and exit criteria to each. A milestone nobody can fail is decoration.

items.title: 3 · Wire the dependencies
items.text: Link the work packages honestly: finish-to-start where truly serial, start-to-start and finish-to-finish where work can overlap. Find the critical path — the longest chain sets the end date.

items.title: 4 · Estimate and load resources
items.text: Durations come from the people doing the work, converted through real availability. Load named people against a resource calendar with holidays and blackout periods marked.

items.title: 5 · Anchor the immovable constraints
items.text: Payroll cycles, year-end blackouts, enrollment windows go in first. Work backward from the payroll calendar to place testing windows, then fit the rest around them.

items.title: 6 · Baseline and control
items.text: Get steering approval on the baseline, then status against it weekly: percent complete, milestone hits and misses, critical-path variance. Re-baseline only with a recorded decision.

content.text: Common Mistakes

items: Starting from the date instead of the work. Backward-scheduling from a fixed go-live without testing fit produces a promise, not a plan.
A WBS with no owner per package. Work without a named owner is work nobody statuses.
Everything linked finish-to-start. Serial plans for parallelizable work stretch the timeline and hide options.
Estimating without availability. Ten person-days at half allocation is four weeks.
Milestones without gates. A milestone nobody can fail is decoration.
Silent re-baselining. Moving dates without a recorded decision erases the project's memory.
Discovering the payroll calendar mid-project. Immovable constraints go in first.

content.label: Plan or date list: spot the difference
beforeItems: Go-live date chosen in a steering deck
Tasks listed, nobody owns them
Everything linked finish-to-start
Durations guessed without availability
Payroll calendar discovered mid-project
Dates moved quietly when they slip
afterItems: End date computed from the work
WBS packages with one named owner each
Dependencies model real parallel work
Estimates converted through resource calendars
Immovable constraints anchored first
Baseline approved; changes logged and approved

content.text: Key Takeaways

items: A real plan is the logic connecting scope to scheduled delivery — dates are the output, never the input.
The WBS enforces completeness: every package estimable, owned by one person, with a clear done criterion.
Milestones mark decisions, gates give them teeth, and the critical path shows where delays move go-live.
Durations come from the people doing the work, converted through real availability.
Payroll cycles, year-ends, and blackouts are schedule anchors that go in first.
Baseline once, measure honestly every week, never re-baseline silently.

content.text: FAQ
How detailed should the plan be?
Detailed enough to status honestly. Packages of days to two weeks, one owner each — weekly truth without administrative bloat.
Who should build the schedule — the project manager or the workstream leads?
Both, in sequence. The leads own the WBS and estimates; the project manager owns dependencies, the critical path, resource loading, and the baseline.
What is the difference between the plan and the methodology?
The methodology structures delivery — phases, gates, roles, governance. The plan schedules the work inside it: tasks, dependencies, dates, resources.
How often should the schedule be updated?
Weekly status, critical-path recomputation with every update, formal review at each phase gate. A stale plan teaches the team to ignore it.
Next Steps

items: Build the WBS with your workstream leads — one owner per package — and run the "what's missing" review before setting dates.
Place milestones at every phase boundary with gate criteria from the delivery methodology.
Map dependencies honestly, find the critical path, and protect it.
Load named resources against real calendars and anchor to the payroll cycle — see the go-live checklist for cutover detail.
Baseline with steering approval, link risks to your risk register, and review the full journey.

title: HCM Implementation Methodology: How Consulting Teams Structure Delivery
excerpt: A practitioner's guide to HCM implementation methodology: phased delivery models, workstreams, governance, and entry/exit criteria that hold.

content.text: Ask an experienced implementation consultant what "methodology" means on an HCM project and you will rarely hear a framework brand name. You will hear something plainer: a way of organizing the work so a hundred moving pieces land in the right order, with decisions made by the right people, and nothing declared "done" before it is. Methodology is the delivery skeleton. Every discipline on this blog — requirements, fit-gap, data migration, UAT, go-live — hangs off it.

Projects without an explicit methodology still run on an implicit one: whoever shouts loudest sets priorities, testing gets compressed whenever the schedule slips, and go-live happens when the money runs out rather than when the system is ready. Making it explicit is what separates professional delivery from hopeful delivery.
What Methodology Covers — and What It Doesn't

Methodology answers three questions: what gets done, in what order, and who decides it is done. It does not answer how the system should be configured or whether a requirement is justified — those live inside the phases. A team debating "agile or waterfall" while requirements are still vague is arguing about the container instead of filling it.

HCM projects are not software development with HR branding: the team configures an existing platform, migrates data into it, and teaches an organization to work differently. So the methodology carries data migration as a first-class workstream, treats payroll cycles as immovable constraints, and builds change management into the plan rather than bolting it on in week twenty.
The Six Phases of HCM Delivery
Most professional HCM delivery models resolve into six phases — firms name them differently, but the sequence is stable because it reflects how the work unfolds.

Initiate. Charter, scope boundary, team, governance model. The real deliverable is alignment: a written agreement on what success looks like, who decides what, and how issues escalate: ambiguities left here become arguments in every later phase.

Design. Requirements gathered, workshops run, states mapped, fit-gap produces the signed design baseline. The most thinking-intensive phase and the most often compressed — protect it: incomplete thinking here just builds the wrong thing faster.

Build. Configuration against the approved design, data migration passes in earnest, integrations wired. Every configuration change traces to a signed design decision; anything else goes through change control.

Validate. System testing, integration testing, then UAT — the client's formal acceptance that the system does what was designed, not a second design phase. This is the strictest gate in the project: no unresolved critical defects, UAT sign-off on record.

Deploy. Cutover, go-live, hypercare opening. The cutover runbook dominates — owners, timings, rollback triggers — with concrete exits: first payroll cycle processed correctly, hypercare issues trending down, support transition begun.
Sustain. Knowledge transfer, support handover, lessons learned, formal closure. Skip it and every future question becomes an escalation to people who have left the project.

Underneath all six phases, three engines run continuously: risk management, data migration readiness, and change management — each with its own cadence, reported at every governance review from initiation to closure.

content.alt: Horizontal diagram of six delivery phases — Initiate, Design, Build, Validate, Deploy, Sustain — each with its deliverables and exit criteria
content.caption: The six delivery phases — Initiate, Design, Build, Validate, Deploy, Sustain — with the Validate gate the strictest in the project.

content.label: Walk the six delivery phases
content.intro: Every HCM implementation moves through the same six phases. Click through to see what each phase owns, produces, and requires before the gate opens.

items.title: 1 · Initiate — charter the project
items.text: The project gets its charter, scope boundary, team, and governance model. Steering committee formed, decision cadence set, first honest draft of the plan. Exit: approved charter and plan, with roles and escalation paths written down.

items.title: 2 · Design — do the thinking
items.text: Requirements gathered, workshops run, current and future states mapped, fit-gap analysis produces the design baseline. The most thinking-intensive phase — and the one most often compressed. Exit: signed-off design baseline approved by the business.

items.title: 3 · Build — configure against the design
items.text: Configuration happens against the approved design, data migration passes begin, integrations get wired. Every change traces to a signed design decision; anything else goes through change control. Exit: a working system in a staging environment.

items.title: 4 · Validate — prove it works
items.text: System testing, integration testing, then user acceptance testing, in that order — plus end-user training. UAT is acceptance of what was designed, not a second design phase. Exit: signed UAT acceptance, zero unresolved critical defects.

items.title: 5 · Deploy — cut over and go live
items.text: Cutover runbook executes step by step with owners, timings, and rollback triggers; hypercare command structure stands up to catch what testing missed. Exit: first payroll cycle processed correctly, support transition begun.

items.title: 6 · Sustain — make it operational
items.text: Knowledge transfer completes, support handover finishes, lessons learned get recorded, the project closes formally. Without documented handover, every future question becomes an escalation. Exit: closure accepted by the sponsor.

content.text: Delivery Models: Waterfall, Agile, and the Hybrid Most Projects Actually Use

The waterfall-or-agile debate is a false binary: different workstreams tolerate iteration differently. Most experienced teams land on hybrid — phased gates at project level, iterative cycles inside the phases — with the model chosen per workstream, not per project.

Waterfall runs the phases sequentially with formal gates. Its strength is predictability — clear plan, budget, and accountability — which suits regulated workstreams like payroll and benefits. Its weakness is late feedback: a design misunderstanding surfaces in UAT, when the cost of being wrong is highest. It assumes requirements are stable: true for payroll tax rules, false for talent management.

Agile builds in iterations with fast feedback, demonstrating working configuration early. It suits workstreams where the process can genuinely evolve — recruiting, performance, learning — where stakeholders see something real every few weeks. The trade-offs: scope drifts without discipline, fixed-price and fixed-date contracts are harder to hold, and it demands constant business availability that clients rarely staff.

Hybrid is the HCM norm, not a compromise. The project keeps its entry/exit gates, steering cadence, and hard constraints (payroll deadlines do not iterate), while configuration happens in short cycles inside Design and Build. The danger is superficial: agile rituals layered over a waterfall mindset — two-week "sprints" that are just task lists, retrospectives nobody acts on. The ritual is easy to copy; the discipline is the methodology.

One rule from experience: payroll should be the most gate-disciplined workstream. It has a legal obligation to be right on a fixed date, it cannot be partially deployed, and errors affect people's pay.

content.alt: Three-column comparison of Waterfall, Agile, and Hybrid delivery models for HCM projects with strengths, trade-offs, and best-fit workstreams
content.caption: Waterfall, Agile, and Hybrid on HCM projects: phased gates at project level, iterative cycles inside the phases — the model follows the workstream.

content.text: The Core Workstreams and Who Owns Them

Phases describe when work happens; workstreams describe who does what, continuously: project management, solution design and configuration, data migration, integrations, testing, change management and training, cutover/deployment. Small projects merge them; large ones split them.

Three roles carry the methodology, and their boundaries matter more than their titles. The project manager owns the plan, schedule, RAID log, and governance cadence. The solution architect owns design integrity — including the authority to reject configurations that break the whole. The workstream leads own their areas end to end: data quality, test discipline, adoption. Where boundaries blur, the same question gets answered three ways, and the project discovers in UAT that nobody owned data quality.

I have seen projects succeed with average people where the boundaries were crisp — and struggle with excellent people where they were not. Clear ownership is a methodology output, not a personality trait: write the RACI in Initiate and enforce it from week one.
Governance and Decision Cadence

Governance is the methodology's nervous system — the rhythm of meetings and decisions that keeps the project honest — working across three levels. The project team tracks tasks, risks, and issues weekly (daily during critical windows). The steering committee — sponsor, key executives, project leadership — meets monthly or at phase gates to decide scope changes, resolve escalations, and approve gate exits. Between them, a design authority handles the steady stream of mid-level decisions.

Two principles keep it functional: decide at the lowest level with the authority to decide — steering sees escalations and gate approvals, not every design question — and record every decision with date, rationale, and owner, or the same questions resurface every few weeks at the cost of another meeting.

The cadence must be real, not ceremonial. A steering committee that meets monthly but never cancels scope is observing, not governing. The test is simple: has a hard decision been made in the last month? If not, there is a governance structure but no governance.
Entry and Exit Criteria: The Gates That Hold

Entry and exit criteria make phases real rather than decorative: an entry criterion states what must be true before a phase begins, an exit criterion what must be true before it ends. Without them, phases bleed together — configuration starts before design is signed, testing starts before the system is stable — and the project loses the ability to stop and fix things at the right moment.

Criteria should be concrete and checkable. "Design is complete" is not a criterion; "gap log signed off by all process owners, design baseline approved by steering" is. For Validate, entry means a stable test environment, reviewed scripts, and loaded test data — UAT never starts on a promise. Exit means signed UAT acceptance and zero unresolved critical defects, not "almost all closed."

The hardest part is holding the gates under schedule pressure: every project reaches a moment where the gate says stop and the timeline says go, and a gate waived under pressure is not a gate. The cost arrives later, usually in hypercare, multiplied. If steering waives an exit criterion, it must record the risk accepted: silent waivers are how projects go live unready.
Common Mistakes

items: Treating methodology as a document instead of a discipline. A methodology deck nobody references after kickoff is decoration; it lives in the gates held, the cadence kept, and the decisions recorded — not the slideware.

Choosing the model for the project instead of the workstream. Declaring the whole project "agile" or "waterfall" ignores that payroll needs gates while talent needs iteration. The model should follow the workstream, not the label.

Starting Build before Design is signed. The most common gate violation, and the most expensive: configuration against an unsigned design is rework waiting to happen — discovered, almost always, in UAT.

Blurring the three roles. When the project manager makes design decisions or the solution architect manages the schedule, the methodology has holes that issues will find. Write the RACI in Initiate; enforce it from week one.

Ceremonial governance. Meetings that inform but never decide, steering committees that observe but never govern. If no hard decision has been made in a month, the governance model is a calendar invite, not a control.
Skipping Sustain. Closing the project without knowledge transfer and documented handover: the implementation succeeds and the operation fails.

content.text: Key Takeaways

items: Methodology answers what gets done, in what order, and who decides it is done — it is the delivery skeleton every other discipline hangs off.
Six phases carry HCM delivery: Initiate, Design, Build, Validate, Deploy, Sustain — with risk, data, and change management running continuously underneath.
The model follows the workstream: phased gates at project level, iterative cycles inside Design and Build; payroll stays the most gate-disciplined workstream.
Three roles carry the methodology — project manager, solution architect, workstream leads — and crisp boundaries between them matter more than titles.
Governance is a real cadence of real decisions: project team weekly, steering at gates, design authority for the mid-level stream — every decision logged.
Entry and exit criteria make phases real; a gate waived silently under pressure always collects its cost later, in hypercare.

content.text: FAQ
What is the difference between a methodology and a project plan?

The plan says what will happen when — tasks, dates, resources. The methodology says how delivery is structured and governed — the phases, the gates, the roles, the decision cadence. The plan lives inside the methodology; a detailed schedule without phase gates and governance is a plan with no way to catch itself going wrong.
Can a small HCM implementation use the same six phases?

Yes — the phases describe the logic of the work, not the size of the team. On a small project, one person may own three workstreams and a phase may last two weeks, but Design still precedes Build, Validate still precedes Deploy, and the exit criteria still gate the transitions. Compress the phases, never skip them.
Who should own the methodology — the client or the consulting partner?

The consulting partner typically brings the methodology, but the client must own the governance. The partner can propose phases and gates; only the client's steering committee can enforce them — approve scope changes, hold exit criteria, accept go-live risk. A methodology the client does not enforce is the partner's fiction.
How does methodology connect to requirements, fit-gap, data migration, and UAT?

They are the content that fills the phases: requirements and fit-gap analysis produce the Design baseline; data migration runs as a workstream across Build and Validate; UAT is the exit gate of Validate; the go-live checklist operationalizes Deploy. Methodology is the structure; the disciplines are what flows through it.
Next Steps

items: Map your project to the six phases — name what each phase owns and produces for your scope, using The Complete Guide to HCM Implementation as the reference journey.
Assign the model per workstream — which workstreams need gates, which need iteration, and who decides.
Write the RACI in Initiate — project manager, solution architect, workstream leads — and enforce it from week one.
Define entry and exit criteria as checkable statements — and protect the Validate gate above all others.
Set the governance cadence now — and link open risks to your risk register.

title: Fit-Gap Analysis in HCM Projects: How to Run It So Design Decisions Actually Stick
excerpt: A practitioner's guide to fit-gap analysis in HCM implementations: running the workshops, categorizing gaps, and making design decisions that stick.

content.text: Every HCM implementation eventually faces the same uncomfortable moment. A requirement — often one everyone assumed was obvious — turns out not to exist in the new system's standard offering. Someone in the room asks, "so can it do that?" and the answer is a pause. What happens in the next ten minutes determines whether the project gets a clean design decision or a compromise that haunts it through testing, go-live, and every upgrade after.

Fit-gap analysis is the discipline that structures that moment. It compares what the organization needs against what the system does out of the box, labels each difference honestly, and forces a decision — adopt the standard process, adapt, or customize — while there is still time to act on it. Done well, it is the cheapest phase of the entire project: decisions made in a workshop cost a fraction of the rework they prevent in UAT. Done poorly, it becomes a ritual where every requirement is declared a "fit" until configuration proves otherwise.
What Fit-Gap Analysis Actually Is

Fit-gap analysis answers one question for every in-scope requirement: does the new system handle this as standard (a fit), or is there a difference that needs a decision (a gap)? That is the whole concept, and the simplicity is the point — it creates a shared vocabulary so the project team, the client, and the vendor are classifying the same reality.

A fit is not the same as "the system can do it if we change it enough." A genuine fit means the standard capability covers the requirement with configuration alone — no code, no bolt-on, no manual workaround carried forward as technical debt. Anything else is a gap, and gaps get decisions, not optimism.

The output of the analysis is a gap log: every gap described, dispositioned, assigned an owner, and signed off. That log becomes the connective tissue of the design phase — configuration teams build from it, testers trace scripts to it, and the steering committee governs scope through it. Without it, the same requirement gets debated three times by three different groups, and the project pays for the same argument repeatedly.
When Fit-Gap Happens — and What It Needs First

Fit-gap sits between requirements and detailed design. It needs three inputs to be worth running. First, a requirements baseline that is precise enough to compare against something — vague requirements ("the system should handle approvals") cannot be matched to capabilities and will produce false fits. Second, an honest understanding of the system's standard capabilities, demonstrated rather than asserted: if the capability has not been shown working, it is not a fit yet. Third, decision-makers in the room — people authorized to change a process or approve a customization, not just describe one.

Run it too early, before requirements exist, and the team classifies wishes. Run it too late, after configuration has started, and the decisions arrive as change orders. The sweet spot is the design window: requirements gathered, current-state maps understood, and the implementation team still able to shape the build.

One scheduling note from experience: separate jurisdiction-specific sessions when the project spans the US and Canada. Payroll rules, statutory deductions, and leave entitlements differ enough that mixing jurisdictions in one fit-gap session doubles the discussion time and halves the decision quality.
The Fit Side: Adopting the Standard Process

Most requirements should be fits, and most fits should stay fits. Modern HCM platforms cover the vast majority of standard HR, payroll, time, and benefits processes well. When a requirement fits, the right move is almost always to adopt the standard process as designed — and to change the organization's process to match it rather than the reverse.

This is the harder conversation of the two, because it asks people to give up familiar ways of working. The case for adoption is practical, not philosophical: every deviation from standard is something the project must build, test, train, and maintain — and something that complicates every future upgrade. The standard process has been tested across thousands of customers; the customized one gets tested by your project team alone.

I have seen fit decisions reversed months later because a stakeholder "just remembered" an exception. The defense is documentation: record the fit, note the standard process adopted, capture who agreed, and move on. Re-litigation is the tax on undocumented decisions, and fit-gap produces plenty of them if the log is not kept current.
The Gap Side: Categorizing Every Gap
Not every gap is equal, and treating them as equal is how customization budgets disappear. Every gap should be classified into one of four dispositions before anyone discusses building anything:

content.alt: Four-panel diagram of gap disposition types — configure, adapt the process, customize, change the policy
content.caption: The four gap dispositions, in order of preference: configure, adapt the process, customize, or change the policy.

items: Configure within standard. The system supports the need through its normal setup — a field, a rule, a workflow definition. This is the cheapest gap to close and the one teams should hunt for hardest. A surprising number of "gaps" dissolve when someone who knows the system deeply looks at the requirement fresh.

Adapt the process. The organization changes how it works to match the system's standard capability. The requirement is real, but the way it is done today is preference rather than necessity. This disposition requires business authority — someone must own the process change — and it is where the most valuable design conversations happen.

Customize. Build something the system does not offer. This is occasionally unavoidable — statutory requirements, genuinely differentiating processes, compliance obligations that cannot be met any other way. But every customization carries a lifetime cost: it must be tested at go-live and re-tested at every upgrade, it needs documentation nobody volunteers to write, and it is the first suspect whenever something breaks. Customization is a decision the project pays for repeatedly.

Change the policy. Sometimes the gap reveals that the requirement itself is the problem — an outdated policy, a rule nobody remembers the reason for, a control that made sense in the legacy system. The cheapest gap to close is the one that should never have existed.

content.text: The discipline is in the order: always test dispositions one and two before reaching for three. Teams that start at "can we customize it?" have skipped the two cheapest answers.

content.alt: Layered flow diagram showing the fit-gap decision path from requirement to adopt, configure, adapt, or customize
content.caption: The fit-gap decision path: every requirement is classified as a fit or a gap, and every gap earns one of four dispositions.

content.label: The four gap dispositions — flip each card

items.back: The system supports the need through normal setup: fields, rules, workflow definitions. The cheapest gap to close. Always test this first.
The organization changes how it works to match the standard capability. Requires real business authority. Where the most valuable design conversations happen.
Build what the system does not offer. Occasionally unavoidable for statutory or compliance needs. Carries lifetime cost: testing at go-live, re-testing at every upgrade.
Sometimes the requirement itself is the problem: an outdated policy or a rule nobody remembers. The cheapest gap to close is the one that should never have existed.

content.text: The Decision Framework: Four Questions for Every Gap
When a gap survives the easy answers, put it through four questions before approving a customization:
Is it legally or compliance-required?

Statutory payroll rules, labor-law obligations, audit and segregation-of-duties requirements — these are non-negotiable and justify investment. A tax calculation that must be exact is not the same category as a preferred report layout.
Is it genuinely business-critical, or is it preference?

Ask what happens if the standard process is used instead. If the honest answer is "people would have to learn something new," that is preference. If the answer is "we would violate a collective agreement," that is critical. The test separates needs from habits.
What does the workaround cost — really?

Sometimes the honest answer is that a small manual step, done monthly by one person, costs less over five years than building and maintaining a customization. Not every gap deserves a system solution; some deserve a procedure. Cost it over the system's lifetime, not the project's.
What is the upgrade and maintenance impact?

Customizations age. Every one of them must be re-validated when the platform updates, and each adds risk to regression testing. A customization that looks cheap in the project budget can be expensive in the support budget for years. Make the decision with the full lifecycle in view.

Run the questions in order, in the workshop, with the decision-makers present. A gap that cannot survive all four should not be customized. A gap that survives them gets a customization with a clear, documented justification — which is an entirely different thing from a customization that happened by default.
Running the Workshop That Produces Decisions

Fit-gap workshops are decision meetings, not demonstrations. The format that works: requirement by requirement, standard capability shown, classification declared, disposition agreed — moving fast enough that the room feels momentum and carefully enough that nothing is glossed over.

Put the right people in the room: process owners who can approve process changes, payroll and compliance leads for the regulated areas, and the consultants who know the system's actual capabilities — not its brochure. Keep groups by process area so discussions stay concrete; a session that mixes time tracking with benefits enrollment will decide neither well.
Three ground rules keep the session productive.

items: No "we'll decide later" without a named owner and a date — parked items are decisions deferred, and deferred decisions become change orders.
The vendor demonstrates; the client decides. If the implementation partner is classifying gaps, the fox is guarding the henhouse — the business team owns every disposition.
Timebox each requirement. A gap debated for forty-five minutes is usually a gap that needs offline analysis, not more debate; park it with an owner and keep moving.

content.text: Documenting the Decisions

A fit-gap analysis that lives in workshop memories is a fit-gap analysis that did not happen. The gap log is the deliverable, and a useful one records: the requirement, the standard capability assessed, the gap description in plain language, the disposition, the owner, the decision date, and the sign-off. One row per gap, no exceptions.

The log then does real work downstream. Configuration teams build against it — every customization in the build traces to a logged, approved gap, which makes unauthorized scope visible immediately. Test planning uses it — customized areas get deeper test coverage because that is where defects concentrate. And the steering committee governs through it: when a new "requirement" appears in UAT, the log answers whether it was decided, deferred, or never raised. That single reference ends more scope arguments than any escalation process.
Common Mistakes

items: Letting the vendor classify the gaps. The implementation partner's incentive is a smooth project, not necessarily the right design. The business team must own every disposition; the partner advises and demonstrates.

Declaring everything a fit. Optimistic fits are the most expensive kind of gap — they are discovered during configuration or testing, when the cost of the real answer is highest. A fit claimed without a demonstration is a gap in disguise.

Treating all gaps as customization candidates. Skipping the configure and adapt dispositions is how projects accumulate technical debt before go-live. The cheapest dispositions should be tested first, every time.

Excluding the people who can say yes. A workshop full of analysts and no decision-makers produces recommendations, not decisions. Every session needs someone authorized to change a process or approve a build.

Analysis paralysis. Fit-gap can become a second discovery phase if the team keeps reopening settled items. Timebox, park with owners, sign off, move on. Perfection in the workshop is the enemy of a decision the project can build on.

No sign-off. An unsigned gap log is a draft, and drafts get re-litigated. Get formal approval of the dispositions before configuration begins — it is the design baseline the whole project builds against.

content.label: Self-check: can you spot the real gap?

questions.q: A payroll clerk wants the new system's pay slip to look exactly like the legacy pay slip, including the company logo placement. The standard pay slip shows all required information. What is this?
questions.why: This tests whether you separate business needs from preferences.

options.text: A gap requiring customization
options.why: The information need is fully met by the standard pay slip.

options.text: A preference, not a gap — adapt the process
options.why: Correct. Nothing business-critical is missing; the layout preference should adapt to the standard.

options.text: A compliance-required gap
options.why: No statutory rule dictates pay slip layout as long as required information is present.

questions.q: The legacy system calculates a province-specific statutory deduction that the new system's standard rules engine does not cover. What disposition applies?
questions.why: This tests the compliance question in the decision framework.

options.text: Adapt the process — use the standard calculation
options.why: Statutory deductions are non-negotiable; the standard process cannot be adopted here.

options.text: Customize, with documented justification
options.why: Correct. Compliance-required and not achievable by configuration: this is a justified customization.

options.text: Change the policy
options.why: Policy cannot override statutory requirements.

questions.q: A fit-gap workshop has debated one requirement for 45 minutes with no agreement. What should the facilitator do?
questions.why: This tests workshop discipline.

options.text: Keep debating until consensus is reached
options.why: Extended debate signals the item needs offline analysis, not more discussion.

options.text: Park it with a named owner and a date, and move on
options.why: Correct. Timebox, assign an owner, keep momentum — the decision comes back with facts.

options.text: Let the vendor decide the disposition
options.why: Dispositions belong to the business team; the vendor advises but does not decide.

content.text: Key Takeaways

items: Fit-gap analysis compares every requirement against the system's standard capabilities and forces a decision on each difference — adopt, adapt, or customize.
It belongs between requirements and design, with a precise requirements baseline and decision-makers in the room.
Every gap gets one of four dispositions: configure, adapt the process, customize, or change the policy — in that order of preference.
Customizations survive four questions: compliance-required, genuinely business-critical, true lifetime workaround cost, and upgrade impact.
The gap log is the deliverable: configuration builds from it, testing traces to it, and the steering committee governs scope through it.

content.label: Fit-gap questions, answered

items.q: How is fit-gap analysis different from requirements gathering?
items.a: Requirements gathering defines what the organization needs. Fit-gap compares those needs against the new system's standard capabilities and decides what changes — the process or the system. Gathering produces the input; fit-gap produces the decisions.

items.q: Who should decide whether a gap gets customized?
items.a: The business — process owners with the authority to change how work gets done, supported by payroll and compliance leads for regulated areas. The implementation partner demonstrates capabilities and estimates effort, but the disposition decision belongs to the client.

items.q: What happens when a gap is found after design sign-off?
items.a: It goes through change control, not the workshop. Late gaps get the same four questions, but with an added one: what does this cost now that design is frozen? Most late "gaps" turn out to be preferences that survived because nobody asked the four questions early enough.

items.q: How many gaps are too many?
items.a: There is no magic number, but the ratio tells a story. If most requirements are gaps, the system selection may have been wrong — or the requirements describe the legacy system rather than the business need. A healthy fit-gap ends with most requirements adopted as standard and a small, justified list of customizations.

content.text: Next Steps

items: Confirm your requirements baseline is precise enough to compare — review the requirements gathering guide.
Run fit-gap by process area with decision-makers present, using the four-question framework for every gap.
Log every gap with its disposition, owner, and sign-off — and link open items to your risk register.
Build traceability from the gap log into configuration and UAT scripts.
Govern scope through the log — and for the full journey, see The Complete Guide to HCM Implementation.

title: Current vs Future State Process Mapping for HCM Implementations
excerpt: A practitioner's guide to current-state and future-state process mapping in HCM implementations: workshops, pitfalls, and design that survives go-live.

content.text: Every HCM implementation lives or dies on a simple question: how does work get done today, and how should it get done on the new system? The discipline that answers it is process mapping — first capturing the current state ("as-is"), then designing the future state ("to-be"). Done well, it produces the single most reliable design artifact a project will ever have. Done poorly, it becomes an expensive exercise in documenting dysfunction, or a future-state map nobody recognizes on go-live day.

I have watched a payroll process that "took ten minutes" unravel into eleven handoffs, three spreadsheets, and two people quietly doing the same reconciliation. I have also seen future-state maps signed off with enthusiasm, then abandoned in week three of hypercare because they described a vendor demo, not the company. This article covers how to do both halves properly — and how to keep the maps alive through build, test, and go-live.
What Current-State Mapping Actually Is

Current-state mapping documents how a process works today: the system entries, the emails, the spreadsheets, the hallway approvals, the "check with Maria first" steps. Not the policy manual version — the version the person doing the work would show you if you sat beside them for a full pay cycle.

It serves three purposes. It creates a factual baseline: what happens, who does what, where the pain lives. It surfaces hidden requirements — exceptions, workarounds, shadow controls — that will break the future-state design if they are discovered in UAT instead. And it earns the design team credibility: when stakeholders see their reality captured faithfully, they trust the future-state conversation that follows.

Capture happens in facilitated discovery workshops: small groups, process by process, walked end to end from trigger to outcome, with the people who do the work in the room. The facilitator keeps asking "and then what happens?" until the process is genuinely complete — noting every manual step, duplicate entry, and "we wait" moment.
The As-Is Trap: Documenting Dysfunction

Almost every project flirts with the same trap: weeks spent producing beautiful as-is maps, then treating them as the design. Consultants call it "paving the cow path" — re-implementing every twist of the current process in the new system. The result is a shiny platform running yesterday's habits, workarounds faithfully rebuilt.

A mid-size company I worked with had a termination process where HR entered the departure in one system, emailed IT, filled a paper form for facilities, then — two weeks later — emailed payroll "just to make sure." The as-is map was accurate. But it was never meant to be the blueprint. Its value was what it revealed: four handoffs, three channels, no confirmation loop, and a two-week lag costing real money in overpaid wages and unreturned equipment. The future-state design collapsed all of it into one workflow with automated notifications and a two-day confirmation control. The as-is map's job was to make that case undeniable — not to become the design.

Treat current-state maps as evidence, not instructions. Their highest purpose is to be argued with. If a participant looks at the as-is and says "that is embarrassing, we should fix that," the session has done its job before the future state even begins.

content.alt: Layered diagram showing the three stages of process mapping: capture the current state, analyze and design, and build the future state
content.caption: The three stages of process mapping: capture, analyze and design, then build the future state.

content.label: Interactive: the same process, before and after

items.heading: The termination process, as mapped
paragraphs: 1. HR enters the departure in the HR system.
2. HR emails IT to revoke system access.
3. HR fills a paper form for facilities to collect equipment.
4. Two weeks pass — no confirmation loop exists.
5. HR emails payroll "just to make sure."
What the map revealed: 4 handoffs, 3 channels, a 2-week lag, and no confirmation loop.

items.heading: The redesigned termination workflow
paragraphs: 1. HR initiates one termination workflow.
2. The system auto-notifies IT, facilities, and payroll — no emails, no paper forms.
3. Each party completes their task inside the workflow.
4. A two-day confirmation control closes the loop.
The redesign: 1 workflow, automated notifications, a 2-day confirmation, and a full audit trail.

content.text: From Current State to Future State: The Design Leap

The as-is to to-be transition is where the real design work happens — and the phase most teams underinvest in. Future-state mapping is not the as-is with a new logo. It is a deliberate redesign grounded in three inputs: the pain points captured in the current state, the standard capabilities of the new system, and the fit-gap decisions about what the organization will change versus what the system must accommodate.

Every future-state step should answer: why is this step here? "Because we have always done it" means challenge or remove it. "Because payroll compliance requires segregation of duties" means it stays — with a control marker. "Because the system can auto-route it" means it becomes a configuration item, not a human task. The map becomes a decision record as much as a flow diagram.

One thing teams routinely miss: the future state must fit how people actually work, not an idealized version. A time-entry process assuming managers approve timesheets every Friday is fiction if half the managers work rotating shifts and approval happens on Mondays. The current-state maps are your reality check — validate the future state against them, or design the change management where it does not fit.
Anatomy of a Good Future-State Map
A map that survives reality has five consistent elements. Walk through each one:

content.label: The five-part anatomy of a future-state map

items.title: Swimlanes
items.text: Horizontal bands for HR, the hiring manager, payroll, IT, the employee — force the handoff question into the open, because every line crossing a lane boundary is a handoff, and handoffs are where processes break.

items.title: Decision points
items.text: Named explicitly: the decider, the criteria, and each branch. Vague "if needed" branches are where test scripts fail.

items.title: Controls
items.text: Get a distinct symbol, turning the map into audit evidence that survives configuration instead of being bolted on afterward.

items.title: Exception paths
items.text: Drawn, not just the happy path: the manager who never approves, the failed bank file, the employee with two positions in two entities. If exceptions live only in someone's head, go-live will find them.

items.title: System actions vs human actions
items.text: The map separates automated workflow, system validations, and genuine human tasks — because that distinction is what the configuration team builds from.

content.alt: Swimlane flowchart example of a future-state new-hire onboarding process with handoffs between HR, the hiring manager, and payroll
content.caption: A future-state swimlane map: every lane crossing is a handoff, and handoffs are where processes break.

content.text: Running a Workshop That Works
Start by agreeing on the trigger and the outcome before drawing a single box. Half of all mapping arguments are really disagreements about where the process starts and ends.

Put the operators in the room, not just their managers. Managers describe the policy; operators describe the reality. The most valuable participants are the ones who say "actually, that is not how it works" — protect them, because they are saving the project from a design based on fiction.

Work at the level where decisions, handoffs, and system interactions change — typically the task level for payroll, the step level for HR service delivery. A useful test: if the map cannot generate a test scenario or a configuration question, it is too high-level. If the workshop drowns, it is too low.

Close with validation: read the map back to the room, walk it end to end, and ask, "if the system worked exactly like this, would it handle your hardest case?" Then get formal sign-off within days, not weeks. Stale maps lose authority; sign-off turns the map into a design commitment the whole project builds against.
Using the Maps Across the Project

Maps earn their cost through reuse. In design, every configuration decision traces to a step on a map. In data migration, the maps reveal which data each process actually needs — the input the migration plan depends on. In testing, every branch, exception path, and handoff becomes a script; UAT coverage can be measured directly against the maps, which is why UAT planning should start from them. In training, the swimlanes become role curricula. In hypercare, "which step on the map failed?" is the fastest diagnostic question you can ask. After go-live, the maps anchor continuous improvement. Maps filed away after design are a sunk cost; maps referenced in every phase are project infrastructure.

content.alt: Layered pyramid showing mapping granularity levels from L1 value chain to L2 process to L3 task detail
content.caption: Map at the right granularity: L1 value chain, L2 process, L3 task detail.

content.text: Common Mistakes

items: Mapping the policy instead of the practice. The manual says approvals happen in the system; operators approve by email and enter it later. Map the manual and your design targets a process that does not exist.
Letting the to-be be the as-is with new labels. Same handoffs, same manual steps, same waits — that is the current state drawn twice, not design. Challenge every step.
Wrong granularity. Too high and the map cannot generate test scenarios; too low and the workshop never finishes.
Forgetting controls. If segregation of duties and audit checkpoints are not on the map, they will not be in the configuration — and an audit is the most expensive place to discover that.
Excluding the operators. Designing with managers alone produces maps of intent. The operators' version comes first.
Skipping sign-off. A map never formally approved is a suggestion, not a design. When scope debates erupt, the signed map settles them.
Filing the maps after design. Reuse them in every phase, or do not bother making them.

content.label: Check your understanding

questions.q: In process mapping, what does "paving the cow path" mean?

options.text: Re-implementing the current process's workarounds and habits in the new system
options.why: The as-is map is evidence, not a blueprint — rebuilding every twist of today's process on a new platform just runs yesterday's habits on shiny software.

options.text: Drawing process maps by hand on paper instead of in a mapping tool
options.why: The as-is map is evidence, not a blueprint — rebuilding every twist of today's process on a new platform just runs yesterday's habits on shiny software.

options.text: Skipping future-state design and going straight to configuration
options.why: The as-is map is evidence, not a blueprint — rebuilding every twist of today's process on a new platform just runs yesterday's habits on shiny software.

options.text: Using swimlanes for every process, even simple ones
options.why: The as-is map is evidence, not a blueprint — rebuilding every twist of today's process on a new platform just runs yesterday's habits on shiny software.

questions.q: Which of these belongs on a good future-state map?

options.text: Only the happy path — exceptions are too rare to draw
options.why: The article's five-part anatomy: swimlanes, named decisions, controls, exception paths, and system-vs-human separation. Drawing only the happy path is exactly the trap the article warns against.

options.why: The article's five-part anatomy: swimlanes, named decisions, controls, exception paths, and system-vs-human separation. Drawing only the happy path is exactly the trap the article warns against.

questions.q: Who should be in a process-mapping workshop?

options.text: Managers only — they know the process best
options.why: The operators who do the work daily, plus their supervisors and every touching function. Managers describe the policy; operators describe the reality — designing with managers alone produces maps of intent.

options.why: The operators who do the work daily, plus their supervisors and every touching function. Managers describe the policy; operators describe the reality — designing with managers alone produces maps of intent.

options.text: Nobody — just document from the policy manual
options.why: The operators who do the work daily, plus their supervisors and every touching function. Managers describe the policy; operators describe the reality — designing with managers alone produces maps of intent.

content.text: Key Takeaways

items: Current-state maps capture how work actually gets done — workarounds included. Their job is to surface pain, not to become the design.
Future-state design is deliberate redesign: every step justifies its existence against pain points, system capabilities, and fit-gap decisions.
Good to-be maps use swimlanes, name decisions, mark controls, draw exception paths, and separate system actions from human ones.
Right workshops: operators plus managers, task-level granularity, sign-off within days.
Reuse the maps in every phase — design, migration, testing, training, hypercare — or the investment is wasted.

content.text: Treat current-state maps as evidence, not instructions. Their highest purpose is to be argued with.
Frequently Asked Questions

content.label: Process mapping questions, answered

items.q: How long should process mapping take?
items.a: Plan on several weeks of workshop time for a mid-size implementation covering core HR, payroll, time, and benefits, plus validation cycles. Rushing mapping compresses the project's most important design thinking into its cheapest window — the savings are almost always false.

items.q: Do we need current-state maps with a "best practice" system?
items.a: Yes, kept lightweight. You need them to find the exceptions, integrations, and compliance obligations the standard process does not cover. You do not need a 200-step map of a process being fully replaced.

items.q: Who should attend the workshops?
items.a: The people who do the work daily, their supervisors, and representatives from every touching function — HR operations, payroll, benefits, IT, finance. Keep groups small, and bring the same participants back for future-state design.

items.q: How do process maps relate to requirements documents?
items.a: They are companions. The map shows flow — sequence, handoffs, decisions, exceptions. The requirements document captures the rules, calculations, and data behind the flow. A map without requirements is a picture; requirements without a map are a list with no context.

content.text: Next Steps

items: Inventory your processes. List the end-to-end processes in scope and agree on each one's trigger and outcome before any workshop.
Plan the workshops with a discovery workshop playbook.
Map, then challenge. Capture the as-is faithfully, then challenge it before designing the to-be.
Design with decisions attached. Every step earns its place; link mapping-surfaced risks to your risk register.
Carry the maps forward into configuration, data migration, UAT, training, and the go-live checklist. For the full journey, see The Complete Guide to HCM Implementation.

title: HCM Implementation Risk Management: A Practical Framework
excerpt: HCM implementations fail on predictable risks. A practical risk management framework — identification, assessment, response planning, and governance — from a PMI Risk Management Professional.

content.text: Most HCM implementations don't fail on technology. They fail on risks everyone saw coming — unclear scope, dirty data, an under-resourced client team, a skipped parallel payroll — that nobody managed as risks. They were discussed in hallways, not tracked in registers.

As a PMI-certified Risk Management Professional (RMP) leading enterprise HCM implementations, I treat risk management as the operating system of the project, not a document produced at kickoff and forgotten. This is the framework I use.

content.alt: Flat-vector illustration of a navy shield deflecting warning markers above a project timeline, symbolizing risk management protecting an HCM implementation
content.caption: A shield over the project timeline: risk management as the operating system of the implementation.

content.text: Why Risk Management Decides HCM Outcomes
An HCM implementation has three properties that make risk management non-optional:

items: 1. Payday is unforgiving. Payroll defects are visible to every employee simultaneously. The cost of a realized risk isn't rework — it's trust.
2. Complexity is multiplicative. Modules × entities × jurisdictions × integrations. Each dimension adds risks that interact.
3. The client team is the constraint. The people who know the legacy system are also running today's payroll. Capacity risk is the silent killer of these projects.

content.text: Projects that manage risk explicitly don't have fewer problems — they have fewer surprises. That difference is what separates on-time go-lives from rescue engagements.
The Risk Management Lifecycle for Implementations
Risk management on an implementation follows a continuous loop, not a one-time exercise:

items: 1. Identify — surface risks early and continuously
2. Assess — score probability and impact honestly
3. Plan responses — assign owners and actions before risks materialize
4. Monitor — review the register on a fixed cadence
5. Control — execute responses and track effectiveness

content.text: The cadence matters more than the template. A simple register reviewed weekly beats a sophisticated model reviewed never.
The 10 Risk Categories Every HCM Project Should Track
Use these categories to make sure identification is complete — most "surprise" risks are just unexamined categories:

items: 1. Scope — Requirements grow after design sign-off
2. Data — Legacy data quality breaks migration
3. Resources — Client payroll lead has no protected capacity
4. Schedule — Dependencies on year-end close freeze the timeline
5. Technology — Integration with benefits carrier fails in testing
6. Compliance — Multi-jurisdiction tax rules misconfigured
7. Change/adoption — Managers don't complete approval training
8. Vendor/partner — Third-party deliverable slips
9. Governance — Steering committee can't reach decisions
10. Cutover — Go-live weekend encounters data freeze issues

content.text: For each category, ask the team: "What would have to be true for this to hurt us?" The answers are your risk list.
How to Build the Risk Register
Every risk entry needs these fields — nothing more, nothing less:

items: Risk statement — written as condition → consequence: "If the legacy time-keeping data is not cleansed before migration, then UAT will surface pay-rule defects late, delaying go-live."
Category — one of the ten above
Probability — High / Medium / Low
Impact — High / Medium / Low (on timeline, cost, quality, or compliance)
Score — probability × impact, mapped to a 1–9 scale
Owner — a named person, not a team
Response plan — what we do, by when
Trigger — the observable event that activates the response
Status — open, mitigated, occurred, closed

content.text: Companion piece: Implementation Risk Register: Template and Field Guide (Oct 7) walks through a filled example.
Assessing Risks: A Simple Scoring Model
Resist the urge to over-engineer. A 3×3 matrix is enough:
3×3 Scoring Matrix

items: High probability x Low impact: 3
High probability x Medium impact: 6
High probability x High impact: 9 (red)
Medium probability x Low impact: 2
Medium probability x Medium impact: 4
Medium probability x High impact: 6
Low probability x Low impact: 1
Low probability x Medium impact: 2
Low probability x High impact: 3
7–9 (red): active response plan, executive visibility, weekly review
4–6 (amber): response plan drafted, owner assigned, biweekly review
1–3 (green): watchlist, reviewed monthly

content.text: Score honestly. The most common failure in risk assessment is grading your own risks leniently because acknowledging a red risk feels like admitting weakness. It's the opposite — red risks with plans are what mature delivery looks like.

content.alt: 3x3 risk scoring matrix mapping probability against impact, with scores 1 to 9 color-coded green for low, amber for medium, and red for high
content.caption: The 3×3 scoring model: probability × impact, from watchlist green to executive-visibility red.

content.text: Response Strategies That Actually Work
Four classic strategies, with implementation-specific notes:

items: Avoid — eliminate the risk. Example: freeze scope after design sign-off with formal change control.
Mitigate — reduce probability or impact. Example: run data-cleansing sprints before migration instead of during testing.
Transfer — shift ownership. Example: contractual SLAs with integration vendors. (Note: you can transfer work, never accountability for payday.)
Accept — for low-score risks, document the acceptance consciously rather than discovering it later.

content.text: The strategy most teams underuse is avoidance through sequencing — restructuring the plan so the risk can't occur. Moving training inside the 3-week pre-go-live window avoids knowledge decay entirely. That's cheaper than any mitigation.

content.alt: Diagram of the four risk response strategies — avoid, mitigate, transfer, and accept — each with an HCM implementation example
content.caption: The four classic response strategies — plus the most underused one: avoidance through sequencing.

content.text: Risk Governance: Who Owns What
Governance Roles

items: Project manager — Maintains the register, drives the review cadence
Risk owners — Execute response plans for their assigned risks
Workstream leads — Identify new risks in their domain continuously
Executive sponsor — Decides on red risks requiring scope, budget, or timeline trade-offs
Steering committee — Reviews top risks at every meeting — first agenda item, not last

content.text: Put risks first on the steering agenda. When risks go last, they get the leftover five minutes, and the register becomes theater.
Common Mistakes Teams Make

items: 1. Writing risks as concerns, not statements. "Data quality" isn't a risk. "If X, then Y" is a risk — it tells you what to watch and what breaks.
2. No named owners. A risk owned by "the team" is owned by no one.
3. Reviewing monthly. On an active implementation, monthly review means risks materialize between meetings. Weekly for red/amber.
4. Hiding red risks from sponsors. Sponsors can't help with risks they can't see. Transparency is the job.
5. Closing risks prematurely. A mitigated risk stays open until the mitigation is verified — the parallel run actually reconciled, the training actually happened.

content.text: Key Takeaways

items: HCM implementations fail on unmanaged known risks, not unknown unknowns.
A simple register reviewed weekly beats a sophisticated model reviewed never.
Write risks as "if X, then Y" with named owners and observable triggers.
Score honestly — red risks with plans are mature delivery, not weakness.
Risks go first on the steering agenda, not last.

content.text: FAQ
What is risk management in an HCM implementation?

The continuous practice of identifying, assessing, planning responses for, and monitoring the uncertainties that could derail the rollout — from scope creep and data quality to resource constraints and cutover failures.
What should an implementation risk register contain?
Risk statements (condition → consequence), category, probability and impact scores, a named owner, a response plan, an observable trigger, and status — reviewed weekly for high-scoring risks.
What are the biggest risks in HCM implementations?
Scope creep, poor legacy data quality, under-resourced client teams, weak executive sponsorship, compressed testing, low user adoption, and multi-jurisdiction compliance complexity.
How often should the risk register be reviewed?
Weekly during active implementation for red and amber risks; the top risks should be the first agenda item at every steering committee meeting.
Who owns risk on an implementation project?
The project manager maintains the register and cadence, named individuals own specific risks, and the executive sponsor decides on trade-offs for the highest-severity risks.
Next Steps
Get the companion Implementation Risk Register Template (Oct 7). Read the Complete Guide to HCM Implementation for the full delivery picture. Planning a rollout or rescuing one? contact Karim.

title: Requirements Gathering for HCM Implementation: A Step-by-Step Guide
excerpt: How to gather requirements for an HCM implementation: stakeholder workshops, process mapping, fit-gap analysis, and writing requirements developers can configure against.

content.text: Bad requirements are the most expensive defect in an HCM implementation. A misunderstood pay rule discovered in UAT costs ten times what it costs in discovery — and if it reaches production, it costs trust.
Requirements gathering is the structured process of capturing what the business needs the system to do, at a level of detail the configuration team can build against. Here's how to do it well.

content.alt: Requirements gathering workshop with process mapping for HCM implementation
content.caption: Workshop-style discovery surfaces the contradictions that one-on-ones miss.

content.alt: Six-step requirements gathering flow for HCM implementation: stakeholders, current state, workshops, requirements, fit-gap analysis, sign-off
content.caption: The six-step requirements gathering flow for HCM implementations.

content.text: Step 1: Identify the Right Stakeholders
Map stakeholders across four groups:

items: Process owners — payroll, benefits, HR operations leads who know the current rules
End users — managers and employees who will live in the system
Compliance — legal/tax for jurisdiction-specific rules
IT — integrations, security, data

content.text: Missing stakeholder groups are the top cause of late requirements. If payroll isn't in the room, payroll rules won't be in the document.
Step 2: Document the Current State

Before designing the future, capture the present: current processes, pain points, workarounds, and the "tribal knowledge" that lives in people's heads. Use simple flowcharts — not to preserve the current state, but to make sure everyone agrees on what it is.
Step 3: Run Structured Workshops
Workshops beat interviews for HCM discovery. Group dynamics surface contradictions ("we calculate overtime weekly" / "no, it's biweekly") that one-on-ones miss.
Run workshops by process area — payroll, time, benefits, core HR — with a fixed agenda: current process, pain points, future-state needs, decisions needed. Timebox ruthlessly and assign a scribe.
Step 4: Write Requirements That Can Be Configured
The test of a good requirement: could a consultant configure the system from it without asking a follow-up question? Compare:

items: Weak: "The system should handle overtime."
Strong: "Overtime is calculated weekly at 1.5× the regular rate for hours over 44/week per Ontario employment standards. Double-time does not apply. The following employee groups are exempt: [list]."

content.text: Every requirement needs: a unique ID, the process area, the rule stated precisely, the source stakeholder, and acceptance criteria.
Step 5: Run Fit-Gap Analysis

Map each requirement against standard system functionality: fit (covered out of the box), gap (needs configuration or workaround), or custom (needs development). Challenge every "custom" — most are preferences, not needs, and each one adds testing surface and upgrade risk.

content.alt: Fit-gap classification diagram: fit (covered out of the box), gap (needs configuration or workaround), custom (needs development)
content.caption: Every requirement classifies as fit, gap, or custom — challenge every custom.

content.text: Step 6: Get Formal Sign-Off

Requirements are baselined with written sign-off from process owners. After sign-off, changes go through change control — with impact assessment on timeline and cost. This single discipline prevents most scope creep.
Common Mistakes

items: 1. Gathering requirements from managers only — the people doing the work know the exceptions.
2. Accepting vague requirements — "flexible approval workflows" means nothing until defined.
3. Skipping the compliance review — jurisdiction rules discovered in testing are redesigns.
4. No traceability — every requirement should trace to a design element and a test case.

content.text: Key Takeaways

items: Requirements quality determines configuration quality — invest in discovery.
Write requirements precisely enough to configure against without follow-up questions.
Fit-gap discipline keeps customizations (and their costs) under control.
Baseline with sign-off; everything after goes through change control.

content.text: FAQ
What is requirements gathering in an HCM implementation?
The structured process of capturing business needs — pay rules, workflows, compliance requirements — at a level of detail the implementation team can configure the system against.
Who should participate in requirements workshops?
Process owners (payroll, HR ops), end users (managers, employees), compliance/legal, and IT. Missing groups cause late requirements.
What is fit-gap analysis?
Mapping each requirement against standard system functionality to classify it as fit (out of the box), gap (configuration needed), or custom (development needed).
How detailed should HCM requirements be?
Detailed enough that a consultant can configure without follow-up questions — specific rules, thresholds, exceptions, and acceptance criteria.
Next Steps
Continue to Solution Design Documents: What Good Looks Like, Fit-Gap Analysis in HCM Projects, or contact Karim.

title: Data Migration in HCM Implementations: A Practical Guide
excerpt: A practical guide to HCM data migration: cleansing legacy HR data, mapping pay codes, test loads, and reconciliation — the phase where implementations are won or lost.

content.text: Ask implementation veterans where projects actually break, and data migration wins the poll. Not the software, not the methodology — the data. Duplicate employee records, inconsistent job codes, accrual balances that don't reconcile: legacy data carries years of accumulated entropy, and migration is where the bill comes due.

content.alt: Data migration flow from legacy HR systems to a new HCM platform with validation checkpoints
content.caption: Migration is the phase where HCM implementations are won or lost — data first, always.

content.text: The Migration Sequence
Every migration follows five steps, in order:

items: 1. Extract — pull data from legacy systems into a staging area
2. Cleanse — fix it before it touches the new system
3. Transform — map legacy structures to new structures
4. Load — import into the target environment
5. Reconcile — prove the load is correct

content.text: Skipping or compressing any step just moves the pain downstream, where it's more expensive.

content.alt: Flow diagram of the five-step HCM data migration sequence: extract, cleanse, transform, load, reconcile
content.caption: The five-step migration sequence — in that order, every time.

content.text: Cleanse Before You Migrate, Not During
The cardinal rule: cleansing happens in step 2, never in step 5. Common defects to hunt:

items: Duplicate employee records (rehires, name variations)
Inconsistent job codes and department names
Missing or invalid tax IDs and banking details
Accrual balances that don't match any source of truth
Terminated employees still flagged active

content.text: Assign data ownership to the business — HR and payroll must validate their own data. IT can move it; only the business can say it's right.
Map Everything Explicitly
Every legacy field needs a documented mapping: source field to transformation rule to target field. Pay special attention to:

items: Pay codes — legacy earnings/deduction codes rarely map 1:1; document every merge and split
Organizational structure — hierarchies drive security, approvals, and reporting
Employment statuses — full-time/part-time/contractor definitions vary by system

content.text: Unmapped fields are a decision to lose data. Make it conscious.
Run Multiple Migration Passes
Plan for at least three loads:

items: 1. Trial load into a test environment — validates the mechanics
2. Full mock load — validates the data, reconciled completely
3. Production load — the real thing, during the cutover window

content.alt: Diagram of the three migration passes — trial load, full mock load, and production load — with defects feeding back into cleansing
content.caption: Plan at least three migration passes — each must be cleaner than the last.

content.text: Each pass should get cleaner. If pass 2 surfaces the same defects as pass 1, the cleansing process is broken — fix the process, not just the data.
Reconcile to the Penny
Reconciliation is not "the headcount looks about right." For each load, reconcile:

items: Employee headcount by status, pay group, and entity
Year-to-date earnings, deductions, and taxes
Accrual balances (vacation, sick, other banks)
Benefits elections and dependent records
